title: Abdullahs Stand for Full Vande Mataram as Congress Urges INDIA Bloc Allies to Follow Suit
excerpt: Omar and Farooq Abdullah stood through all six stanzas of the national song at a Srinagar film festival, exposing a rift within the opposition alliance over the Vande Mataram debate.
body:
• Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister Omar Abdullah and National Conference president Farooq Abdullah stood for the full rendition of Vande Mataram at the inaugural International Film Festival in Srinagar.
  • Congress general secretary K C Venugopal expressed displeasure, urging allies to honour the 1937 resolution and sing only the first two stanzas.
  • The National Conference pushed back sharply, with NC leader Bashir Ahmed saying alliance partners cannot dictate terms on the national song.
  • The BJP praised the Abdullahs and attacked Congress, with spokesperson Sudhanshu Trivedi calling the party the "Muslim League of the 21st century."

A fresh fault line has opened within the opposition INDIA Bloc after Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister Omar Abdullah and his father, National Conference president Farooq Abdullah, stood through the complete rendition of Vande Mataram at the inaugural International Film Festival in Srinagar on Tuesday.

The Abdullahs were seen standing throughout the national song’s full three-minute performance — all six stanzas — in line with the Union Home Ministry’s new guidelines. The move put them visibly at odds with the Congress party, their principal alliance partner, which last month resolved to sing only the first two stanzas at all party events.

Congress Reacts With Displeasure

Congress general secretary (organisation) K C Venugopal responded swiftly, posting on X that “the full version of Vande Mataram sits uneasily with the syncretic and pluralist ethos that our freedom fighters envisioned and nurtured for India.”

https://x.com/TimesNow/status/2097386262479208795

“For us, the considered judgment of Mahatma Gandhi, Pandit Nehru, Sardar Patel, Subhash Chandra Bose, Rajendra Prasad, Acharya Narendra Dev, Maulana Azad, Sarojini Naidu and J B Kripalani — shaped in no small part by the counsel of Gurudev Rabindranath Tagore — remains paramount.”

— K C Venugopal, Congress General Secretary

The Congress Working Committee had decided last month to abide by the 1937 resolution on Vande Mataram, which adopted only the first two stanzas as the national song. Venugopal urged allies to honour the wisdom of the freedom fighters and join the party in singing only that version, calling it a deliberate choice “to keep the song from being communalised.”

National Conference Fires Back

The National Conference responded firmly, rejecting any suggestion that alliance partners could dictate conduct on the national song. NC leader Bashir Ahmed said Venugopal “has the right to tweet, but can’t impose” his party’s position on allies.

“As alliance partner you can’t dictate terms whether to sing or how much to sing. It is people’s choice. We are against imposing anything on people,” Ahmed said.

Congress MP Pawan Khera took a more conciliatory line, saying the party hoped others “including our allies” would follow the two-stanza practice “because these two stanzas work to unite the country.” But Congress leader Kapil Singh escalated further, accusing the Abdullahs of bowing to the “Nagpur diktat” — a reference to the RSS headquarters — rather than respecting the Congress position.

BJP Seizes the Moment

The ruling BJP moved quickly to exploit the opposition split. BJP MP and spokesperson Sudhanshu Trivedi praised the Abdullahs and launched a broadside against Congress, calling it the “Muslim League of the 21st century” and accusing it of surrendering to “fundamentalist forces.”

CPI Rajya Sabha MP P. Santosh offered a measured response, noting that every political party has the right to its own position while cautioning against unnecessary escalation. JMM spokesperson Manoj Pandey echoed the sentiment, saying all parties should respect each other’s views.

A Recurring Flashpoint

The Vande Mataram debate has been a recurring feature of Indian politics. Union Home Minister Amit Shah launched a scathing attack on Congress last month, calling its two-stanza decision “anti-national” and aimed at “appeasing its vote bank.” Congress hit back through senior leader Jairam Ramesh, who labelled BJP leaders “fraudulent nationalists.”

The latest episode underscores the fragility of the INDIA Bloc’s internal cohesion on cultural and identity issues, even as its constituent parties attempt to present a united front on economic and governance matters. With the BJP holding a clear majority in Parliament, these visible rifts within the opposition carry political costs that extend well beyond the symbolism of a national song.
